Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Program Upgradability
Program Upgradability and Versioning
Understand when to keep programs mutable, how upgrades work, and how to migrate on-chain data safely.
In this lesson
  • Compare immutable and upgradeable BPF loaders and why you might choose one.
  • Learn the program data / buffer / upgrade authority trio that enables upgrades.
  • Walk through a deploy → upgrade workflow and a versioned data migration example.
Coming up: code walkthrough, CLI commands, migration strategy, and best practices.
Explore Key Topics
BPF Loaders
Immutable vs Upgradeable tradeoffs and when to pick each.
Upgrade Workflow
Buffer upload, finalize, and program upgrade commands.
Data Migration
Use version fields and conditional deserialization to preserve state.
Concept Map
Program ID (stable)
Public key users call; stays the same across upgrades.
Program Data Account
Holds executable bytes; owned by BPF Loader Upgradeable.
Buffer Account
Temporary store for new bytecode during an upgrade.
These pieces let you patch code without changing program identity, reducing user migration risk.

screens.title: Why Upgradability Exists
screens.narratorSegment: Upgradability exists because software evolves. Immutable programs are attractive for trust and auditability — once deployed they cannot change — but that same immutability makes bug fixes and new features painful. If you must add a feature or patch a vulnerability, users must migrate their accounts and interactions to a new program ID, which is disruptive and error-prone. Solana provides the BPF Loader Upgradeable as a practical middle ground: the program ID stays stable while the executable bytes live in a program data account that the loader can replace. This preserves user-facing addresses while allowing controlled updates. A concrete example is a token program with a bug in fee calculation; patching it without changing the program ID avoids forcing every token account owner to reinitialize state. A common misconception is that upgradability removes the need for audits — it does not. Upgrades are a frequent attack vector, so combine audits, multisig authorities, and testnet rehearsals. To summarize: immutability buys trust, upgradability buys flexibility. Plan which property you need before you choose how to deploy. Why Upgradability Exists means upgradability lets a program's executable bytes be replaced while keeping the same public program id.. In practical terms, tradeoffs between immutable and upgradeable programs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Upgradability lets a program's executable bytes be replaced while keeping the same public program ID.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Why Upgradability Exists
Definition & tradeoffs
Immutable programs offer maximum trust; upgradeable programs allow fixes and feature additions without changing program identity.
Example
A deployed token program with a fee bug can be patched by upgrading bytes while keeping all token accounts intact.
Common misconception
Having an upgrade path eliminates the need for audits. In reality, upgrades increase attack surface and require rigorous review and multisig protection.
Key Takeaway
Choose immutability for maximal trust; choose upgradeability when you need the ability to fix bugs or add features without user migration.
Analogy
Think of program ID as a building's street address and the program data account as the interior layout. Upgrading is like renovating the interior while keeping the address unchanged so people can still find it.
Why it matters
  • Reduces user friction during fixes and feature releases.
  • Makes iterative development on mainnet feasible with careful controls.
  • Requires operational security for upgrade authority handling.

screens.title: BPF Loader vs BPF Loader Upgradeable
screens.narratorSegment: Solana supports multiple BPF loaders; the two you must know are the original BPF Loader and the BPF Loader Upgradeable. The original loader creates immutable program accounts. Once deployed, bytecode cannot change and the program becomes a fixed artifact — great for maximal trust and reproducible audits. In contrast, the BPF Loader Upgradeable splits responsibilities: the program ID remains the stable public key that other programs call, while the actual executable bytes live in a program data account owned by the upgradeable loader. This indirection allows the loader to replace the executable bytes when an authorized upgrade is performed. A concrete example: using the upgradeable loader you can deploy a payment program, later patch a critical bug, and leave all existing payment accounts untouched. A common misconception is that upgradeable programs make on-chain data automatically forward-compatible; they do not. Data structures owned by your program must be migrated explicitly or guarded with version-aware deserialization. When deciding which loader to use, balance immutability’s trust with the operational flexibility of controlled upgrades. BPF Loader vs BPF Loader Upgradeable means original bpf loader → immutable. bpf loader upgradeable → stable program id with replaceable executable bytes via a program data account.. In practical terms, what changes when you pick the upgradeable loader. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Loader Comparison
Original BPF Loader
Deploys immutable programs. Use when you want a fixed, auditable contract that cannot be changed.
Pros
  • Maximal trust and reproducible bytecode guarantees.
  • Removes upgrade-related attack surface.
Cons
  • Any bug or feature requires deploying a new program and migrating users.
BPF Loader Upgradeable
Keeps program ID stable while storing executable bytes in a program data account that the loader owns and can replace.
Pros
  • Enables in-place upgrades without changing user-facing program ID.
  • Supports operational patching and iterative development on mainnet when controlled.
Cons
  • Requires secure management of upgrade authority and migration logic for data changes.

screens.title: Program ID, Program Data Account, and PDA Indirection
screens.narratorSegment: A reliable mental model for upgrades depends on three pieces. First, the program ID is the public key that clients and other programs call. It remains stable across upgrades. Second, the program data account stores the actual executable bytes; it is owned by the BPF Loader Upgradeable system program. Third, the loader uses a derived address relationship so the program ID is essentially a PDA linked to the program data account. That indirection allows replacing bytes without changing the public program key. A concrete scenario: when you deploy, the CLI uploads a buffer then finalizes it into the program data account and returns both the program ID and the program data address. If you later upgrade, the loader replaces the data inside the program data account with bytes from a buffer account. A common misconception is thinking program data is a normal user account under your program; it is not — it is owned by the system loader, which enforces upgrade semantics. Understanding ownership and PDA derivation helps you reason about which accounts your program can access and which are controlled by Solana’s runtime.

keyIdea.title: Ownership rule
keyIdea.text: The program data account is owned by the BPF Loader Upgradeable program, not by the program's own ID, enabling controlled replacement of executable bytes.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Program Identity
Component architecture
Program ID (stable) ← derived PDA relationship → Program Data Account (executable bytes owned by loader).
Program ID
Public key users interact with; address remains constant across upgrades.
Program Data Account
Holds bytecode. Owned by the loader so the loader can change the bytes when authorized.
Buffer Account
Temporary storage for new bytecode during upgrade preparation.
Concrete note
When you deploy with the CLI, expect to receive a program ID and program data address. Save both; the latter is useful for auditing and understanding ownership.
Misconception check
Do not assume program-owned accounts can change the program data. The loader manages program data ownership and must perform upgrades.

screens.title: Deploying a Program with the Upgradeable Loader
screens.narratorSegment: Deploying a program with the upgradeable loader is a small sequence of actions that the CLI automates. First, the CLI uploads your compiled. so to a buffer account. This buffer is a temporary account owned by the loader that stores the raw bytes. Second, the CLI finalizes the buffer into a program data account and derives or assigns a program ID that will be the stable address for your program. The deploy command also sets the deploying wallet as the initial upgrade authority unless you specify a different keypair. Practical example: running the deploy command returns both a program ID and a program data address — you should record them. The misconception to avoid is thinking deploy simply writes bytes to a single account; it actually creates and links buffer, program data, and program ID artifacts under the loader’s ownership model. Finally, treat the upgrade authority like a sensitive operational secret: consider using a multisig in production, or set authority to None if you want immutability after testing. Testing this deploy flow on devnet first is essential before pushing to mainnet.

keyIdea.text: Deploy uploads bytes to a buffer, finalizes into a program data account, and assigns a program ID while setting an upgrade authority.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Deploy Process
Deploy Process (high level)
The CLI performs buffer upload, finalize, and authority assignment steps in sequence.
Step 1
Upload buffer
CLI writes bytes to a temporary buffer account owned by the loader.
Step 2
Finalize
Buffer becomes a program data account and a stable program ID is associated.
Step 3
Set authority
Deploying wallet becomes upgrade authority unless changed.
CLI example
solana program deploy ./dist/counter_v1.so
# returns Program Id and Program Data Address; save them
Tip: always save the program data address in addition to the program ID for audits and ownership checks.

screens.title: Upgrading an Existing Program
screens.narratorSegment: Upgrading replaces the program data account's bytes with code from a buffer account you prepare. The safe workflow is: compile new code, upload it to a fresh buffer account using the write-buffer command, then call the upgrade command which instructs the loader to copy bytes from that buffer into the program data account. The upgrade command requires the upgrade authority's signature — this is how Solana enforces who can change executable bytes. A concrete sequence: compile your updated Rust code to a new. so, run solana program write-buffer to get a buffer address, then solana program upgrade --final --keypair. The --final flag closes the buffer after upgrade. A common mistake is reusing an existing buffer rather than creating a fresh one, or losing the upgrade authority keypair. In production, prefer a multisig upgrade authority; that reduces single-key risk. Also rehearse the upgrade on devnet and confirm your program's behavior with existing accounts after the upgrade completes. Upgrading an Existing Program means upload new bytes to a buffer, then invoke upgrade with the upgrade authority to replace the program data account's bytes.. In practical terms, write-buffer and upgrade steps using the upgrade authority. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › Upgrade Process
Upgrade workflow
Prepare a buffer, then upgrade the program data account using the upgrade authority.
Step A
Compile
Build your updated Rust program to produce a new .so file ready for upload.
Step B
Write buffer
Use solana program write-buffer to upload bytes to a new buffer account and note its address.
Step C
Upgrade
Call solana program upgrade with the program ID, buffer, final flag, and upgrade authority keypair.

screens.title: Initial Counter Program: counter_v1.rs
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the initial counter program and point out the data layout and initialization behavior. The CounterAccount struct contains a value field and a version field. The program checks ownership of a provided account and deserializes that account into CounterAccount. If the version is zero or indicates uninitialized state, the program sets value to 0 and writes version equal to 1. Each invocation increments the value and serializes the updated struct back to the account. This is a clear, simple pattern: a version field allows the program to recognize uninitialized or older-format accounts so that later migration logic can run. A practical pitfall to avoid is changing the struct layout in a new release without adding migration code; deserialization will fail if the data size or field order changes. In our hands-on activity you will deploy this v1 program, create an account with sufficient space, invoke the program several times to increment the counter, and fetch the raw account data to confirm changes. That real evidence helps you validate that the versioning approach works as intended. Initial Counter Program: counter_v1.rs means include a version field even in the first release to enable safe conditional migrations later.. In practical terms, account struct, initialization, and increment logic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.3 › counter_v1.rs
Key code (data struct and flow)
<-- excerpt from counter_v1.rs -->
use borsh::{BorshDeserialize, BorshSerialize};

#[derive(BorshSerialize, BorshDeserialize, Debug)]
pub struct CounterAccount {
  pub value: u32,
  pub version: u8, // Version field
}

// process_instruction: deserialize, init on version 0, increment value, serialize back
Example action
Create a counter account with enough space, call the program multiple times to increment, then fetch and deserialize to confirm version is 1 and value increments.
Did you know?
Even simple structs benefit from an explicit version field. It makes future migrations explicit and easier to test.
Pitfall
Changing field order or sizes without migration causes deserialization errors and program crashes.

screens.title: Upgrading to counter_v2.rs with Migration
screens.narratorSegment: Now examine the upgraded counter that introduces last_updated_timestamp and migrates older accounts. The new CounterAccount adds a 64-bit timestamp and advances version to 2. On invocation the program deserializes the account and checks the version field. If it sees a version less than 2 it fills the new timestamp field with the current clock timestamp and sets version to 2, logging that migration occurred. After migration the regular increment and timestamp update proceed. This pattern is concrete and safe: conditional deserialization recognizes older layouts and transforms them into the new shape before regular logic runs. An important example step is testing the very first invocation after upgrade — you should see a migration log and then subsequent invocations should show only increments and timestamp updates. A common misconception is to rely only on client-side migration; instead embed migration logic in the program so any caller triggers consistent state updates. Always test migrations on devnet with multiple account shapes to confirm backward compatibility. Upgrading to counter_v2.rs with Migration means use a version field and conditional deserialization to initialize new fields on first access after an upgrade.. In practical terms, adding a timestamp field and migrating old accounts. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Upgrade Authority and Operational Security
screens.narratorSegment: The upgrade authority is the designated keypair or multisig that is allowed to initiate upgrades for a program. When you deploy with the upgradeable loader, the deployer becomes the initial authority unless you set a different key. Operationally this authority is a high-value secret: if it is compromised, an attacker could replace your program bytes and introduce malicious logic. For production deployments prefer assigning a multisig as the upgrade authority, which requires multiple parties to approve an upgrade and reduces single-key risk. Another option once you reach a stable release is to set the upgrade authority to None, which makes the program immutable and removes the ability to upgrade entirely; this is a valid strategy when trust and auditability are paramount. A common misconception is that frequent upgrades are safe as long as testing is performed; testing helps but does not remove the need for secure authority management and audits. Consider backups for authority keypairs, restricted storage, and multisig governance for any program with user value. Upgrade Authority and Operational Security means treat the upgrade authority as a critical secret; prefer multisig or removing authority after stabilization.. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we’ll build a clear mental model for why upgradability matters on Solana and how the BPF Loader Upgradeable makes it practical. You will learn why immutable programs can be safe but often impractical, how the program ID and program data account separate identity from bytecode, and what role a buffer account and upgrade authority play during an upgrade. I’ll give a concrete deployment example and a hands-on activity that walks through deploying a simple counter program, then upgrading it to add a timestamp field while preserving on-chain state. We’ll highlight common pitfalls you must avoid: forgetting data migration logic and losing control of the upgrade authority. By the end you’ll be able to explain the deploy and upgrade commands, outline a migration strategy using a version field, and reason about when to make a program immutable. Think about a program you maintain — what would break if you couldn’t upgrade it? That question will guide the exercises ahead.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why program upgradability exists on Solana and pick an appropriate loader for a deployment. You will be able to name and describe the three accounts involved in an upgrade — the program ID, the program data account, and the buffer account — and explain the role of upgrade authority. You will learn to run the deploy and upgrade CLI commands and interpret the addresses they return. Finally, you will be able to design a data migration plan for on-chain accounts, including adding a version field and conditional deserialization logic. Each objective is practical: you’ll use the CLI to deploy a versioned counter, then upgrade it with migration code. These skills matter because upgrades are a regular part of maintaining live programs. Getting comfortable with the mechanics reduces risk, prevents deserialization errors, and helps you choose when to lock a program’s authority to make it immutable.

We will also structure your learning so it progresses from comprehension to practical mastery. First you will learn to explain why upgradability exists and name the loader types. Next you will understand the account relationships and authority model that make upgrades possible. Then you will apply that knowledge by running a deploy and an upgrade in a controlled devnet environment. Finally you will master data migration by writing conditional deserialization and testing upgrades against existing account data. This progression matters because simple familiarity is not enough — upgrades touch both executable code and persistent data. Practicing on a testnet and using a multisig upgrade authority are practical steps that convert understanding into reliable, secure behavior in production settings. Consider each milestone as a checkpoint in your migration plan: verify addresses, test migration logic, and audit the upgrade authority configuration.

Upgradability exists because software evolves. Immutable programs are attractive for trust and auditability — once deployed they cannot change — but that same immutability makes bug fixes and new features painful. If you must add a feature or patch a vulnerability, users must migrate their accounts and interactions to a new program ID, which is disruptive and error-prone. Solana provides the BPF Loader Upgradeable as a practical middle ground: the program ID stays stable while the executable bytes live in a program data account that the loader can replace. This preserves user-facing addresses while allowing controlled updates. A concrete example is a token program with a bug in fee calculation; patching it without changing the program ID avoids forcing every token account owner to reinitialize state. A common misconception is that upgradability removes the need for audits — it does not. Upgrades are a frequent attack vector, so combine audits, multisig authorities, and testnet rehearsals. To summarize: immutability buys trust, upgradability buys flexibility. Plan which property you need before you choose how to deploy. Why Upgradability Exists means upgradability lets a program's executable bytes be replaced while keeping the same public program id.. In practical terms, tradeoffs between immutable and upgradeable programs. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Solana supports multiple BPF loaders; the two you must know are the original BPF Loader and the BPF Loader Upgradeable. The original loader creates immutable program accounts. Once deployed, bytecode cannot change and the program becomes a fixed artifact — great for maximal trust and reproducible audits. In contrast, the BPF Loader Upgradeable splits responsibilities: the program ID remains the stable public key that other programs call, while the actual executable bytes live in a program data account owned by the upgradeable loader. This indirection allows the loader to replace the executable bytes when an authorized upgrade is performed. A concrete example: using the upgradeable loader you can deploy a payment program, later patch a critical bug, and leave all existing payment accounts untouched. A common misconception is that upgradeable programs make on-chain data automatically forward-compatible; they do not. Data structures owned by your program must be migrated explicitly or guarded with version-aware deserialization. When deciding which loader to use, balance immutability’s trust with the operational flexibility of controlled upgrades. BPF Loader vs BPF Loader Upgradeable means original bpf loader → immutable. bpf loader upgradeable → stable program id with replaceable executable bytes via a program data account.. In practical terms, what changes when you pick the upgradeable loader. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A reliable mental model for upgrades depends on three pieces. First, the program ID is the public key that clients and other programs call. It remains stable across upgrades. Second, the program data account stores the actual executable bytes; it is owned by the BPF Loader Upgradeable system program. Third, the loader uses a derived address relationship so the program ID is essentially a PDA linked to the program data account. That indirection allows replacing bytes without changing the public program key. A concrete scenario: when you deploy, the CLI uploads a buffer then finalizes it into the program data account and returns both the program ID and the program data address. If you later upgrade, the loader replaces the data inside the program data account with bytes from a buffer account. A common misconception is thinking program data is a normal user account under your program; it is not — it is owned by the system loader, which enforces upgrade semantics. Understanding ownership and PDA derivation helps you reason about which accounts your program can access and which are controlled by Solana’s runtime.

Deploying a program with the upgradeable loader is a small sequence of actions that the CLI automates. First, the CLI uploads your compiled. so to a buffer account. This buffer is a temporary account owned by the loader that stores the raw bytes. Second, the CLI finalizes the buffer into a program data account and derives or assigns a program ID that will be the stable address for your program. The deploy command also sets the deploying wallet as the initial upgrade authority unless you specify a different keypair. Practical example: running the deploy command returns both a program ID and a program data address — you should record them. The misconception to avoid is thinking deploy simply writes bytes to a single account; it actually creates and links buffer, program data, and program ID artifacts under the loader’s ownership model. Finally, treat the upgrade authority like a sensitive operational secret: consider using a multisig in production, or set authority to None if you want immutability after testing. Testing this deploy flow on devnet first is essential before pushing to mainnet.

Upgrading replaces the program data account's bytes with code from a buffer account you prepare. The safe workflow is: compile new code, upload it to a fresh buffer account using the write-buffer command, then call the upgrade command which instructs the loader to copy bytes from that buffer into the program data account. The upgrade command requires the upgrade authority's signature — this is how Solana enforces who can change executable bytes. A concrete sequence: compile your updated Rust code to a new. so, run solana program write-buffer to get a buffer address, then solana program upgrade --final --keypair. The --final flag closes the buffer after upgrade. A common mistake is reusing an existing buffer rather than creating a fresh one, or losing the upgrade authority keypair. In production, prefer a multisig upgrade authority; that reduces single-key risk. Also rehearse the upgrade on devnet and confirm your program's behavior with existing accounts after the upgrade completes. Upgrading an Existing Program means upload new bytes to a buffer, then invoke upgrade with the upgrade authority to replace the program data account's bytes.. In practical terms, write-buffer and upgrade steps using the upgrade authority. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the initial counter program and point out the data layout and initialization behavior. The CounterAccount struct contains a value field and a version field. The program checks ownership of a provided account and deserializes that account into CounterAccount. If the version is zero or indicates uninitialized state, the program sets value to 0 and writes version equal to 1. Each invocation increments the value and serializes the updated struct back to the account. This is a clear, simple pattern: a version field allows the program to recognize uninitialized or older-format accounts so that later migration logic can run. A practical pitfall to avoid is changing the struct layout in a new release without adding migration code; deserialization will fail if the data size or field order changes. In our hands-on activity you will deploy this v1 program, create an account with sufficient space, invoke the program several times to increment the counter, and fetch the raw account data to confirm changes. That real evidence helps you validate that the versioning approach works as intended. The upgrade authority is the designated keypair or multisig that is allowed to initiate upgrades for a program. When you deploy with the upgradeable loader, the deployer becomes the initial authority unless you set a different key. Operationally this authority is a high-value secret: if it is compromised, an attacker could replace your program bytes and introduce malicious logic. For production deployments prefer assigning a multisig as the upgrade authority, which requires multiple parties to approve an upgrade and reduces single-key risk. Another option once you reach a stable release is to set the upgrade authority to None, which makes the program immutable and removes the ability to upgrade entirely; this is a valid strategy when trust and auditability are paramount. A common misconception is that frequent upgrades are safe as long as testing is performed; testing helps but does not remove the need for secure authority management and audits. Consider backups for authority keypairs, restricted storage, and multisig governance for any program with user value.
